routes.description: Establish a likelihood comparison in which life-permitting fine-tuning is substantially more expected given classical perfect-being theism than given the complete admissible space of single-universe naturalistic alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it grounds the fine-tuning datum, supplies a defensible expectation of valuable conscious life under perfect-being theism, and shows that hypothesis augmentation, simulation, aggregated alternatives, and naturalistic parsimony do not erase the comparative evidential advantage.

motionBridge.description: Show that the posterior-confirming force of fine-tuning remains strong after the relevant theistic and naturalistic hypothesis spaces are compared.

centralBridges.description: Establish that life-permitting conditions are far less expected under single-universe naturalism than under a perfectly good creator with reasons to value conscious moral life.
Explain why admissible alien, simulation, time-travel, or fine-tuning-specific naturalistic alternatives do not collectively neutralize the likelihood asymmetry.
Justify an intrinsic-probability treatment under which the coherence or simplicity of perfect-being theism offsets the specificity of augmented naturalistic rivals.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Provide a principled basis for empirical evidence to discriminate between theism and broad naturalistic alternatives despite logical compatibility with multiple causes.
Account for naturalism's ontological economy and explain how it should be balanced against the claimed conditional-probability advantage.

routes.description: Undercut the strong-evidence inference by challenging the specification and aggregation of the rival hypothesis spaces, the predictive content of divine psychology, and the status of apparent fine-tuning as an objective datum.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if theism cannot be assigned a sufficiently reliable likelihood advantage over the full naturalistic alternative space, or if uncertainty about priors, divine intentions, or the fine-tuning datum prevents the asserted strong confirmation.

motionBridge.description: Show that fine-tuning does not strongly discriminate in favor of God once hypothesis-space ambiguity and uncertain theistic predictions are included.

centralBridges.description: Require comparison with the aggregated space of admissible naturalistic explanations rather than with a selectively austere naturalistic hypothesis.
Establish that perfect goodness and other divine attributes do not yield sufficiently determinate predictions about creating life-permitting conditions.
Show that aggregation, modesty, coherence, and ontological parsimony leave the relevant intrinsic-probability comparison unresolved.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Demonstrate how apparently purposive or religious evidence can remain compatible with broad naturalistic agency explanations.
Test whether apparent fine-tuning is an objective feature requiring explanation or instead a sign that the operative physical theory is defective.

sections.title: The Fine-Tuning Datum and the Core Likelihood Comparison
sections.rationale: This section contains the motion's foundational issue: whether life-permitting parameters constitute an objective and improbable datum whose likelihood differs substantially between classical theism and single-universe naturalism.

sections.title: Naturalistic Alternatives and the Relevant Comparison Class
sections.rationale: The strength of the inference depends on whether theism must outperform one austere naturalistic hypothesis or the aggregated space of alien, simulation, time-travel, and other admissible naturalistic explanations.

sections.title: Divine Goodness, Agency, and Predictive Expectations
sections.rationale: A likelihood advantage for theism requires a defensible bridge from perfect divine goodness to the creation of valuable conscious life, while the opposing burden tests whether divine intentions remain too indeterminate.

sections.title: Intrinsic Probability, Coherence, Modesty, and Parsimony
sections.rationale: This issue determines how the prior plausibility of perfect-being theism compares with disjunctions of limited or augmented naturalistic hypotheses before the fine-tuning evidence is incorporated.

sections.title: Empirical Discrimination and Religious Ambiguity
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether broad alternative explanations make empirical evidence persistently ambiguous and whether such ambiguity undercuts fine-tuning without foreclosing every possible non-empirical argument concerning God.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Life-permitting parameters are extremely improbable under single-universe naturalism but less surprising if a perfectly good God values conscious moral life, so fine-tuning confirms theism.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Miles the floor, and the uninterrupted first-person opening presents his announced fine-tuning argument.

response.rationale: This constructive opening supplies the debate's foundational likelihood comparison and therefore has no earlier opposing locked move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops the foundational comparison and states the intended confirmation inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative proposition is recoverable, but the relevant naturalistic measure and the strength of God's predicted preference remain only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The excerpt strongly asserts a likelihood asymmetry, while its measure assumptions and divine-preference bridge receive limited qualification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The Bayesian direction is coherent, but material bridges from goodness to creation and from parameter ranges to probabilities remain compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt identifies parameter scarcity and valuable conscious life, but does not defend the probability measure or compare serious rival families.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, this directly supplies the indispensable likelihood-asymmetry step, though it does not complete the full motion route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opening advances its own positive comparison rather than interpreting a meaningful opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts a very small naturalistic probability with a less surprising theistic expectation grounded in moral value and conscious agents.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Evidence of intelligent design or an expressed peaceful intention does not securely identify a benevolent source, since a deceptive agent could produce the same apparent signs.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex continues his uninterrupted opening and explicitly maps the benevolent-alien thought experiment onto Miles's proposed spectacular theistic evidence.

components.text: Whether perfect divine goodness makes a life-permitting world materially more expected than it is under naturalism.
Whether apparent purposive signs can establish intentional agency more securely than benevolent character.

response.rationale: The deceptive-agent analogy bears on inferring benevolence from signs, but the pro move stipulates a perfectly good God and needs a goodness-to-creation likelihood bridge; that decisive bridge is not directly answered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, the analogy supplies substantial contrary material but misses the stipulated divine-goodness prediction at issue.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between evidence of intentionality and evidence of benevolence is clear, stable, and expressly probabilistic.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker carefully claims weaker evidence for benevolence rather than impossibility and expressly marks comparative uncertainty.

charity.alternative: The signal could be genuine evidence of both intentional agency and benevolent purpose.
charity.decisiveQualification: Evidence for benevolence can remain substantially weaker than evidence for intentional production.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The intentionality-versus-benevolence distinction is consistent and the deceptive-agent possibility appropriately limits identification of character.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The thought experiment supplies a clear countermodel, though it does not establish representative probabilities for divine action or deception.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it attacks a major divine-psychology bridge, but its mismatch with stipulated perfect goodness limits its position.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move grants that benevolence receives some support while preserving the decisive difference in evidential strength.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says the signal is strong evidence of intelligent intentional production but much weaker evidence of benevolent intentions.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Advanced aliens, future time travelers, and simulators form a disjunctive naturalistic alternative whose combined probability must be compared with theism.
moves.attributionBasis: Alex announces three naturalistic explanations and completes his opening by explicitly stating how their probabilities should be aggregated for comparison.

components.text: Whether the naturalistic likelihood denominator must aggregate multiple admissible alternatives rather than use one austere hypothesis.

response.rationale: The move directly contests the pro comparison class by introducing several naturalistic explanation families and requiring their probabilities to be combined.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive rival-space component but does not yet quantify or defend the combined probability.

precisionFindings.rationale: The aggregation demand is recoverable, though the admissibility boundaries and mutual relations among the alternatives are not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Comparing the aggregate is a legitimate demand, but merely listing alternatives does not yet warrant a strong conclusion about their total probability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Aggregation is a coherent challenge to selective comparison, with a bounded gap concerning overlap and individuation of the alternatives.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete alternatives are supplied, but their priors, likelihoods, independence, and aggregate weight remain materially undefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the move squarely advances the indispensable full-hypothesis-space requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily constructs an expanded comparison class rather than developing a detailed interpretation of the pro argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: The source passage announces multiple naturalistic explanations, including advanced aliens, as components of a broader comparative alternative.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Allowing a tailored natural disposition to match any observation would defeat every possible empirical case for theism, an implausibly sweeping consequence of the stalking-horse method.
moves.attributionBasis: Following the moderator's handoff, Miles explicitly returns to his first response and develops the claimed overgeneralization before asking Alex about it.

components.text: Whether unrestricted tailoring of naturalistic alternatives illegitimately neutralizes every possible item of empirical theistic evidence.
Whether deceptive-agent possibilities specifically weaken inferences from purposive signs to benevolent character.

response.rationale: The reductio directly challenges the unrestricted method of adding tailored naturalistic alternatives, but it does not answer the separate benevolence-identification distinction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive methodological concern but leaves the specific probability and admissibility of the listed rivals unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reductio is clear, but it shifts from defeating strong or decisive evidence to defeating any empirical evidence without an explicit scope qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that the method eliminates every possible empirical case outruns the supplied analogy and conflates compatibility with lack of evidential force.

charity.alternative: Broad naturalistic alternatives may reduce or prevent decisive discrimination without making every observation evidentially inert.
charity.decisiveQualification: Logical compatibility with a rival does not by itself eliminate comparative evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The stated consequence follows only if the skeptical method treats any compatible tailored rival as a complete defeater, a substantial unsupported conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies a methodological reductio but no representative demonstration that the opponent applies the method without prior or likelihood constraints.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly attacks persistent empirical ambiguity, though its overbroad formulation weakens the contact.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reductio notices an important overreach risk but presents the skeptical position more sweepingly than its strongest probabilistic interpretation requires.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the stalking-horse reply would apply to any observation and therefore would rule out every possible empirical line of evidence for theism.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: A consequential fine-tuning argument must specify its theistic hypothesis and show that it explains the evidence better than every admissible naturalistic version, not merely one selected rival.
moves.attributionBasis: The alternating dialogue and Alex's first-person framing identify this sustained answer as his response to Miles's question about possible comparative evidence.

components.text: Whether the legitimate evidential demand is comparative performance across specified theistic and naturalistic hypotheses, not absolute empirical decisiveness.
Whether the original likelihood comparison covers every admissible naturalistic version and a sufficiently specified theistic hypothesis.

response.rationale: The move explains why the absolute-evidence reductio uses the wrong demand and replaces it with a specified full-family comparative test that preserves the evidential issue.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within justified reframes, it explicitly identifies and replaces the overbroad demand while retaining the proper comparative question.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative burden is clear, though 'every admissible version' lacks a fully stated admissibility and aggregation rule.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The demand for broad comparison fits the motion, but literal comparison with every version requires qualifications about grouping and relevance.

charity.alternative: The pro argument may seek confirmation rather than a uniquely decisive explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Confirmation still requires a fair comparison with the relevant aggregate rival space, not logical elimination of all rivals.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The replacement demand follows coherently from comparative confirmation, with a bounded ambiguity about how exhaustive families are individuated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological warrant is plausible and explained, but the excerpt does not establish an operational aggregation rule for the full family.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it states the hypothesis-space completion requirement in nearly its strongest form.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the pro argument's comparative ambition while insisting on a broader and properly specified hypothesis test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The passage distinguishes an uninteresting existence claim from a consequential comparison and requires specification of hypotheses across the rival family.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: The relevant claim compares classical perfect-being theism with every hypothesis consistent with single-universe naturalism, understood as the causal natural order exhausting relevant reality.
moves.attributionBasis: Miles explicitly agrees, then states the precise comparative thesis he means to defend and specifies both his naturalism and classical-theism hypotheses.

components.text: Whether the pro thesis specifies both its theistic hypothesis and the full class of naturalistic hypotheses it claims to outperform.
Whether aliens, simulations, and similar alternatives fall inside the stated single-universe naturalistic comparison class.

response.rationale: The move directly accepts the strong comparative burden, defines the two broad hypotheses, and claims superiority over every naturalistic version within its stated boundary.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the decisive specification demand, although it asserts rather than demonstrates universal superiority.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move expressly limits naturalism to a single universe and defines the perfect-being theistic comparator with stable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparison class is carefully specified, but claiming superiority to any consistent hypothesis is much stronger than the support supplied here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The definitions and comparative commitment are consistent, but no inference here establishes superiority over every member of the defined family.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt gives useful specification but provides little evidence or warrant for the universal comparative conclusion it announces.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly answers the indispensable rival-space specification demand.

representationalCharity.rationale: This move chiefly clarifies and commits to its own comparison class rather than assessing a live opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines single-universe naturalism, claims superiority over any hypothesis consistent with it, and identifies classical perfect-being theism.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: General theism predicts a particular resurrection no better than general alienism because both posit powerful agents whose intentions remain largely unknown.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained skeptical turn answers Donahue's appeal to historical fit and contrasts the two intentional-agent hypotheses.

components.text: Whether empirical events can favor general theism when the intentions of both divine and naturalistic agents remain unspecified.
Whether specifying broad worldview classes supplies sufficiently determinate likelihoods for particular intentional events.

response.rationale: The alien comparison directly supplies a reason why broad agent hypotheses need intention specifications before a particular resurrection receives a likelihood advantage.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive empirical-likelihood issue but addresses one event rather than every possible evidential case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison between general theism and general alienism is clearly limited to predicting a specified resurrection event.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move makes a comparative underdetermination claim and openly conditions it on broad hypotheses with unknown intentions.

charity.alternative: A benevolent creator could make revelation or resurrection more expected than generic aliens would.
charity.decisiveQualification: That advantage requires an additional bridge from benevolence to the particular revelatory act.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from unspecified agency intentions to weak prediction of a particular act is coherent, with only a bounded omitted comparison of plausible motives.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The resurrection example clearly illustrates underdetermination, though one example does not establish persistent ambiguity across all evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it strongly advances empirical ambiguity through a concrete intentional-agent comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accommodates the possible theistic bridge while correctly locating the unresolved work in specifying intentions.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt observes that a benevolent supernatural agent can perform the event but does not directly entail intending it, then invokes aliens as a parallel.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Perfect divine goodness provides some basis for expecting revealed religion and resurrection, whereas a generic alien hypothesis supplies no comparable expectation without added specificity.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly invokes divine benevolence to answer the preceding comparison between unknowable divine and alien intentions.

components.text: Whether perfect divine goodness supplies a non-arbitrary likelihood bridge to revelation and resurrection that generic alien agency lacks.
Whether benevolent character can provide predictive content beyond bare intentional agency.

response.rationale: The move directly answers the unknown-intentions objection by proposing perfect goodness as a reason to expect revealed religion in the relevant historical context.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive intention bridge but only asserts its plausibility and does not defend its comparative magnitude.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly modest: revelation and the specified resurrection are said to have higher probability, not to be entailed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker uses cautious comparative language appropriate to the limited goodness-to-revelation warrant supplied.

charity.alternative: Generic aliens might also have reasons to stage or cause the observed event.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro claim is comparative and requires only some goodness-based advantage, not exclusion of alien motives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative inference is intelligible, but the bridge from perfect goodness to revealed religion remains a material implicit premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Historical context is invoked, but the goodness-to-revelation expectation and the absence of comparable alien motives are substantially asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks divine-psychology underdetermination, though the bridge remains underdeveloped.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly preserves alien compatibility while identifying a proposed reason for a likelihood difference.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt claims that Jesus's resurrection in its life context is more likely on perfect-being theism because revealed religion becomes more probable.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Perfect-being theism occupies a substantial share of general design possibilities, while a life-directed augmented-naturalistic hypothesis occupies an extremely small share of general naturalistic possibilities.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker redirects explicitly to fine-tuning and develops the pro side's Bayesian comparison in a continuous explanatory turn.

components.text: Whether the full comparison should weight specific augmented-naturalistic rivals by their conditional share within general naturalism.
Whether aggregating life-directed alternatives gives them substantial prior probability within the broader naturalistic family.
Whether perfect-being theism has a sufficiently large conditional share within general design possibilities.

response.rationale: The move addresses aggregation by proposing conditional prior shares for specific naturalistic and theistic refinements, though the numerical or structural basis remains undeveloped.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive prior-weighting issue but does not establish the alleged asymmetry across the complete families.

precisionFindings.rationale: The intended conditional-prior comparison is recoverable, but 'general design,' simplicity, and shares of possibility space lack stable measures.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claimed extreme asymmetry is much stronger than the qualitative simplicity comparison and unspecified possibility measures warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional-prior strategy is coherent in outline, but comparing undefined shares across different super-hypotheses leaves a substantial inferential gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The crucial claims of an extremely small naturalistic share and substantial theistic share rely mainly on assertion about simplicity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly addresses the indispensable intrinsic-probability comparison despite weak support.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move principally develops a positive prior comparison rather than presenting a detailed alternative interpretation for evaluation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt assigns very low prior probability to any specific life-directed naturalistic version and claims perfect-being theism is simpler within general design.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Broad naturalistic simulation and science-fiction possibilities can accommodate nearly any observation, preventing such evidence from decisively separating naturalism from theism.
moves.attributionBasis: The skeptical turn follows the terminology exchange and states Malpass's own allocation of simulation hypotheses within naturalism.

components.text: Whether broad rival compatibility removes comparative evidential support rather than merely preventing logically decisive proof.
Whether simulation and science-fiction hypotheses fall within a sufficiently broad naturalistic class to remain empirically compatible.

response.rationale: The move supports persistent compatibility and lack of decisive proof, but the pro objection concerned whether any comparative empirical evidence remains; that decisive distinction is not contacted.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it strongly bears on ambiguity but conflates complete decisiveness with ordinary comparative evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly about complete decisive separation, though 'almost anything' leaves the observational scope somewhat open.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cautious suggestion that decisive separation may be unavailable fits the broad compatibility argument and acknowledges uncertainty.

charity.alternative: Evidence can favor one worldview without ruling the other out completely.
charity.decisiveQualification: Persistent compatibility blocks decisive proof but does not by itself block a likelihood ratio favoring one side.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The compatibility conclusion follows from sufficiently flexible scenarios, but the stronger evidential underdetermination implication needs a likelihood bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Simulation possibilities illustrate compatibility, yet their prior weight and capacity to match likelihoods across observations are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly develops empirical ambiguity, with the proof-versus-evidence conflation limiting its position.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move materially under-engages the strongest probabilistic reading by answering in terms of complete decisiveness.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says naturalistic science-fiction worlds can accommodate almost anything and therefore may prevent completely decisive separation of the worldviews.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: A simulation hypothesis is independently skeptical and merely relocates fine-tuning to base reality because a simulator would probably reproduce the basic physical laws instantiated in the simulation.
moves.attributionBasis: The pro speaker corrects the simulation classification and provides two explicit objections before returning to empirical discrimination.

components.text: Whether simulation hypotheses genuinely explain fine-tuning or merely transfer the same explanatory demand to base reality.
Whether simulation deserves material weight within the aggregated naturalistic rival family.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges simulation's explanatory contribution through a base-reality regress, but it does not answer the broader set of flexible naturalistic possibilities.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the principal simulation component while leaving aliens, time travel, and other flexible rivals untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The regress objection is clear, but the assertion that simulators probably reproduce our basic laws lacks an explicit scope condition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Saying simulation literally explains nothing outruns the unsupported probability claim about base reality and simulator design choices.

charity.alternative: A simulation could implement laws unlike those of base reality and explain observed parameters through simulator selection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such an account needs an independently motivated simulator and base-level conditions rather than mere logical possibility.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress follows only under the material unsupported premise that the simulator probably reproduces the same relevant laws.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: No evidence or defended warrant supports the claim about simulator behavior, making the central factual conditional speculative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly attacks one important source of empirical ambiguity and rival-space expansion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies a real regress concern but weakens the strongest simulation alternative by assuming replicated laws.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt claims a simulator would probably reproduce the simulation's basic laws and thus reduplicate fine-tuning in base reality.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: The disjunction of every specifically limited alternative may have greater total prior probability than a single unlimited hypothesis, reversing the alleged simplicity advantage of the unlimited hypothesis.
moves.attributionBasis: The alternating turn structure and direct answer to Donahue's question identify Malpass as the speaker throughout this response.

components.text: Whether an unlimited perfect-being hypothesis retains a simplicity advantage after all specifically limited alternatives are aggregated.

response.rationale: The move directly reverses the pro conditional-prior comparison by emphasizing that a disjunction sums the priors of many limited alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive aggregation issue but does not justify the prior distribution over limits.

precisionFindings.rationale: The disjunctive argument is recoverable, though the domain of limits and treatment of overlapping hypotheses remain partly unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that the disjunction massively swamps the unlimited hypothesis lacks a defended prior measure over the possible limits.

charity.alternative: An unlimited hypothesis might receive a simplicity or coherence premium exceeding the combined limited alternatives.
charity.decisiveQualification: Aggregation alone does not determine the result without a justified allocation of prior mass.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Summing mutually exclusive alternatives is coherent, but the conclusion needs defended exhaustiveness, exclusivity, and prior assignments.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The decisive swamping claim is asserted without representative priors or a principled measure over the family of limits.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly targets intrinsic-prior ambiguity through the key disjunctive aggregation issue.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges the simplicity intuition but understates the unresolved prior-measure question that could preserve it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The passage contrasts one unlimited hypothesis with a disjunction of all limited hypotheses and says their summed probability swamps the former.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: The modesty of a disjunction of limited alternatives does not by itself show that it outranks theism intrinsically, because coherence may carry greater prior-probability weight than modesty.
moves.attributionBasis: Donahue explicitly interprets Draper's published analysis, describes its two probability factors, and states his own objection to its conclusion.

components.text: Whether the modesty gained by aggregating limited alternatives necessarily outweighs the unlimited hypothesis's claimed coherence.

response.rationale: The move directly identifies an omitted competing prior factor and denies that modesty alone settles the aggregated comparison.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive one-factor inference but does not independently establish coherence's magnitude.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is clearly comparative, although 'coherence' and 'modesty' remain technically underdefined in the excerpt.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that modesty has not been shown to outweigh coherence fits the absence of a defended weighting rule.

charity.alternative: The aggregate of limited hypotheses may be much more modest and therefore receive greater prior mass.
charity.decisiveQualification: That conclusion still requires showing modesty outweighs any coherence difference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The undercutting inference is sound: identifying an unweighted competing factor defeats a conclusion based only on modesty.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt fairly identifies the missing weighting premise, but offers little positive support that coherence actually dominates.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks resolution of the intrinsic-prior comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately reconstructs the aggregation argument and isolates the specific comparative premise it regards as unsupported.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explains the limited-hypothesis disjunction's modesty and objects that its cited analysis merely asserts modesty outweighs coherence.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Naturalism's ontological economy may offset theism's advantages in coherence or modesty because theism adds supernatural commitments to the natural reality it also posits.
moves.attributionBasis: Following Malpass's acceptance of Donahue's point, the same turn introduces a final counterconsideration and contrasts what the two worldviews posit.

components.text: Whether ontological parsimony supplies an independent naturalistic prior advantage even if modesty or coherence favors theism.
Whether theism's claimed simplicity within design offsets its additional supernatural ontology.

response.rationale: The move concedes the preceding factor comparison provisionally and introduces ontological economy as a distinct counterweight to theism's alleged prior advantage.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it adds a material counterfactor but does not supply a rule for balancing ontological and structural simplicity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed parsimony consideration is clear, but what each worldview posits and how ontology is counted remain partly unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker cautiously offers parsimony as a possible offset or route to a draw, which fits the limited support.

charity.alternative: Theism may explain or ground natural reality rather than simply adding one entity to an otherwise identical ontology.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even so, its supernatural commitment requires a defended compensating simplicity or explanatory benefit.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Parsimony is a relevant independent factor, but the additive-ontology premise and tradeoff with other simplicity dimensions remain underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument relies on a compressed inventory of commitments rather than a defended account of comparative ontological cost.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly supplies the required naturalistic-parsimony counterweight.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move notices possible balancing benefits but somewhat compresses the strongest theistic account into simple additive ontology.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says theism posits natural reality plus further supernatural commitments and cautiously proposes that parsimony may offset modesty losses.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Apparent fine-tuning may be a property indicating a defect in the operative physical theory rather than an objective feature of the universe that requires a design explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator-established closing order makes this Malpass's closing, and the speaker explicitly presents a deflationary interpretation associated with Dan Linford.

components.text: Whether apparent fine-tuning is an objective universe-level datum rather than evidence that the operative physical theory is defective.

response.rationale: The closing move directly attacks the status of the datum presupposed by the foundational likelihood comparison by offering a theory-defect interpretation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive datum-status premise but offers the alternative tentatively and without detailed physics.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents a deflationary possibility and uses appropriately cautious language given the limited supporting detail.

charity.alternative: Fine-tuned parameters may be genuine features of the universe even if current theories are incomplete.
charity.decisiveQualification: A theory-defect diagnosis requires identifying which apparent tunings arise from the theory rather than observed reality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The alternative interpretation coherently undercuts the datum premise, with a bounded missing bridge from theory sensitivity to this case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it nearly maximally contacts the explicit datum-status bridge.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning cannot reliably favor theism when divine goodness, values, reasons, and resulting choices are too uncertain to ground a determinate likelihood for a life-permitting universe.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Malpass's closing turn and explicitly develops his previously mentioned objection from uncertainty about divine psychology.

components.text: Whether perfect goodness yields a sufficiently determinate expectation that God would choose a life-permitting universe.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive divine-psychology component but does not fully analyze perfect-goodness concepts offered by the pro side.
